book.title: Meditations
book.author: Marcus Aurelius
book.blurb: The private notebook of a Roman emperor, written to himself on campaign. Short, sharp reminders on how to live well, act justly and meet whatever comes with a steady mind.

chapters.title: Debts of Gratitude
chapters.theme: What Marcus learned from family, teachers and friends.

chapters.title: Time Is Short
chapters.theme: Put off nothing. Act as if each action were your last.

chapters.title: The Guiding Spirit
chapters.theme: Guard the inner part of you that reasons and chooses.

chapters.title: The Inner Retreat
chapters.theme: You can always withdraw into yourself and find calm.

chapters.title: Rising to Work
chapters.theme: You were made to do the work of a human being.

chapters.title: One Fabric
chapters.theme: All things are woven together. Do your part in the whole.

chapters.title: The Wrestler's Art
chapters.theme: Living is closer to wrestling than to dancing.

chapters.title: The Unconquerable Mind
chapters.theme: A mind free of passion is a fortress.

chapters.title: Injustice Is Impiety
chapters.theme: We were made for one another. Wronging others wrongs nature.

chapters.title: Good, Modest, True
chapters.theme: Live up to the names you have given yourself.

chapters.title: The Branch and the Tree
chapters.theme: Stay joined to the community you grew from.

chapters.title: The Final Act
chapters.theme: Three acts can be the whole play. Leave the stage well pleased.

quizzes.q: Book One is mostly a list of what?
options: What Marcus learned from the people around him
quizzes.why: Book One lists what he owes to family, teachers, friends and the gods.

quizzes.q: Which teacher first gave Marcus the writings of Epictetus?
quizzes.why: Rusticus 'gave me of his own' his copy of Epictetus's moral commentaries.

quizzes.q: From his grandfather Verus, Marcus learned to be…
options: Gentle and meek, free from anger
quizzes.why: 'Of my grandfather Verus I have learned to be gentle and meek, and to refrain from all anger.'

quizzes.q: 'Betimes in the morning say to thyself…' What should you expect to meet that day?
quizzes.why: He prepares for difficult people and reminds himself they are kin who cannot truly harm him.

quizzes.q: True or false: Marcus thanks the gods for things he did NOT do, as well as for things he had.
quizzes.why: His thanks to the gods includes the mistakes and temptations he was spared.

quizzes.q: Book Two opens by reminding Marcus of what?
options: How long he has put off these things
quizzes.why: 'Remember how long thou hast already put off these things…'

quizzes.q: How should you go about every action, according to Book Two?
options: As if it were your last action
quizzes.why: Do each action 'as thy last action, free from all vanity'.

quizzes.q: If you lived three thousand years, what could you actually lose?
quizzes.why: No one can lose the past or the future, only the present he is living now.

quizzes.q: Complete the line: 'Remember that all is but ___.'
quizzes.why: 'Remember that all is but opinion and conceit.'

quizzes.q: Theophrastus judged which sins to be worse?
quizzes.why: Sins of desire are worse than sins of anger, which come with pain.

quizzes.q: Why must we hurry, according to the start of Book Three?
options: Our understanding may fail before our body does
quizzes.why: Life wastes daily, and the mind may start to dote before death comes.

quizzes.q: Hippocrates cured many sicknesses and then…
quizzes.why: Healers, astrologers and conquerors all died in their turn.

quizzes.q: What does Marcus warn against spending your days thinking about?
quizzes.why: 'Spend not the remnant of thy days in thoughts and fancies concerning other men.'

quizzes.q: A physician keeps instruments ready for sudden cases. What should you keep ready?
quizzes.why: Keep your principles at hand for whatever comes, divine or human.

quizzes.q: True or false: Marcus says anything that makes you break faith or lose your modesty can still be profitable.
quizzes.why: 'Never esteem of anything as profitable' that makes you break faith or lose modesty.

quizzes.q: Where is the best place to retire to for rest?
quizzes.why: 'A man cannot any whither retire better than to his own soul.'

quizzes.q: If reason is common to all men, what follows?
options: All men are equal in wealth
The world is like one city
quizzes.why: Shared reason means shared law, so the world is, in a sense, one city.

quizzes.q: Thinking of the times of Vespasian, what do you see?
options: The same things as today: marrying, quarrelling, dying
quizzes.why: Every age repeats the same busy scenes, and all of them pass.

quizzes.q: Marcus says you should be like a promontory of the sea. Why?
options: Because it is high and proud
Because it stands firm while the waves break around it
quizzes.why: Stand steady while the waves beat against you, and the water around you settles.

quizzes.q: Complete the line: 'Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself ___.'
quizzes.why: Without the opinion 'I am wronged', the hurt disappears.

quizzes.q: When you are unwilling to rise in the morning, what should you remember?
options: That you rise to do the work of a man
That the day will be short
quizzes.why: Ants, bees and spiders do their part. You were made to do the work of a human being.

quizzes.q: The best kind of giver is compared to what?
options: A vine that bears grapes and seeks nothing more
quizzes.why: Like the vine, he does good and moves on without keeping score.

quizzes.q: Complete the idea: 'Such as thy thoughts are, such will thy ___ be.'
quizzes.why: The soul takes its colour from its thoughts.

quizzes.q: What doesn't hurt the city cannot hurt…
quizzes.why: That rule helps you judge whether you have really been harmed.

quizzes.q: According to Book Five, who 'lives with the gods'?
options: Whoever keeps his soul content with what is given and does what his inner spirit wills
quizzes.why: Living with the gods means being content with your lot and following the spirit within you.

quizzes.q: How does Marcus suggest you see a purple robe or fine food?
options: As what it really is: sheep's wool dyed in shellfish blood, dead fish and birds
As a gift of the gods
quizzes.why: Strip things bare to see what they are and lose their false glamour.

quizzes.q: Someone at the palestra scratches you and breaks your head. What then?
options: Don't hold it against him or suspect him
quizzes.why: Treat it as part of the game and, as with life, without grudges.

quizzes.q: Alexander of Macedon and his mule driver, once dead…
quizzes.why: Death made them equal. Both returned to the same source.

quizzes.q: Marcus wrote: 'As Antoninus, my city is Rome; as a man, my city is…'
quizzes.why: He belonged to Rome and to the whole community of reasoning beings.

quizzes.q: True or false: 'If something is hard for you, you should not think it impossible for a human being.'
quizzes.why: If it is possible for a human, it is within your reach too.

quizzes.q: What should you say to yourself about wickedness?
options: It is what you have already seen many times
quizzes.why: There is nothing new under the sun. Evil is old and familiar.

quizzes.q: How should you treat things that might happen in the future?
options: Don't let them trouble you; you'll meet them with the same reason you have now
quizzes.why: The reason you use today will be there when they come.

quizzes.q: The art of living is more like a wrestler's than a…
quizzes.why: Life means standing firm against unexpected blows.

quizzes.q: What did Epicurus say about pain?
options: It is neither intolerable nor eternal
quizzes.why: Pain that is severe is short. Pain that lasts is bearable.

quizzes.q: 'He is a better wrestler than I.' What should you ask instead?
options: Is he more modest, kinder or more patient?
quizzes.why: Compete in virtue, not in strength.

quizzes.q: Before every action, what question should you ask?
options: How will this affect me, and will I regret it?
quizzes.why: 'How will this suit me? Shall I not repent of it?'

quizzes.q: No time to read? What can you still do?
options: Check your pride, rise above pleasure and pain, and not be angry
quizzes.why: Practising virtue never needs spare time.

quizzes.q: The bitter cucumber teaches you to…
options: Set it away and move on without asking why it exists
quizzes.why: 'Is the cucumber bitter? set it away… Let this suffice.'

quizzes.q: The mind free from passion is compared to what?
quizzes.why: A mind free of passion is an unconquerable stronghold.

quizzes.q: A man who cuts himself off from the whole is like what?
options: A hand or foot severed from the body
quizzes.why: He makes himself a severed limb, though he may still rejoin.

quizzes.q: Book Nine opens by saying the unjust man is also…
quizzes.why: Nature made us for one another, so injustice offends against nature itself.

quizzes.q: 'This day I did come out of all my trouble.' What correction follows?
options: I cast it out: it was never outside, but in my own opinions
quizzes.why: Trouble lived in his judgements, so he threw it out.

quizzes.q: What is 'loss', really?
quizzes.why: 'Loss and corruption is in very deed nothing else but change and alteration.'

quizzes.q: When someone's shamelessness offends you, what should you ask?
options: Can there be a world without shameless men?
quizzes.why: Such people must exist. Don't demand the impossible.

quizzes.q: In sickness, what did Epicurus talk about?
quizzes.why: He kept his mind on philosophy instead of his disease.

quizzes.q: Book Ten opens by addressing whom?
quizzes.why: 'O my soul, the time I trust will be, when thou shalt be good, simple…'

quizzes.q: What names should you take on and keep?
quizzes.why: Live up to these names, and don't trade them away.

quizzes.q: The spider proud of catching a fly is compared to whom?
options: A conqueror proud of capturing men
quizzes.why: Proud conquerors are spiders bragging about flies.

quizzes.q: Whoever grieves over worldly things is like what?
options: A pig squealing as it is slaughtered
quizzes.why: Complaining doesn't change what happens. Only the reasoning creature can accept it freely.

quizzes.q: True or false: Even the best man will have someone glad to see him die.
quizzes.why: No man is so happy in his death that no one rejoices at it. So go gently.

quizzes.q: What is a branch cut off from its neighbour also cut off from?
quizzes.why: Breaking with one person cuts you off from the whole community.

quizzes.q: Book Eleven gives how many 'remedies' for anger?
quizzes.why: 'These nine particular heads, as so many gifts from the Muses…'

quizzes.q: What did the Pythagoreans do first thing in the morning?
quizzes.why: They looked at the stars, which always keep their order, purity and simplicity.

quizzes.q: Which fable does Marcus mention?
options: The country mouse and the city mouse
quizzes.why: He uses it to show how anxiety comes with ambition.

quizzes.q: 'Will any contemn me?' What is Marcus's answer?
options: Let them look to that; I will look to doing nothing worthy of it
quizzes.why: Their contempt is their business. Your conduct is yours.

quizzes.q: Book Twelve says you can have what you aspire to when?
options: Now, if you forget the past and turn to the present
quizzes.why: 'Whatsoever thou doest hereafter aspire unto, thou mayest even now enjoy.'

quizzes.q: Marcus wonders why each person loves himself best, yet values what?
options: Others' opinion of him more than his own
quizzes.why: We love ourselves most, yet care more about what others think of us.

quizzes.q: Complete the line: 'Cast away from thee ___, and thou art safe.'
quizzes.why: Cast away opinion and you come safely into harbour.

quizzes.q: What image shows that there is one common soul?
options: One light of the sun, though walls break it up
quizzes.why: Many walls divide the sunlight, but there is only one sun.

quizzes.q: If your life ends early, what does Marcus say about the play?
options: Three acts can be the whole play
quizzes.why: Leave the stage well pleased, for the one who dismisses you is also pleased.
